Good morning—thank you for making time for this. I’m Dr. Patel, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to check in on how moms are feeling after baby arrives, because the postpartum weeks can throw a lot of emotional curve-balls.

Today I’ll be using the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression and anxiety that sometimes creep up after childbirth. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; there are no right or wrong feelings.

Ready to start?

1. Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
Oh, I’ve actually been able to laugh—like last night my husband made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper and I found myself giggling. It felt nice, almost normal.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as loudly as before, but little moments with my husband or the baby’s silly expressions still make me smile.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to stuff—like my mom bringing dinner tomorrow or taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice. They’re small things, but they feel good to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of being a newborn, not something I did wrong. I might shrug and try a different hold or a burp, but I don’t beat myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay when he’s napping, even though I can see his chest moving. It’s quick—like a little jolt—then I remind myself he’s fine and it passes.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicky feeling—just the little worries about him that fade once I check on him.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I’m keeping up fine. There’ve been a couple moments—like when the baby had a blow-out right before company arrived—where I felt a bit flustered, but I took a breath and handled it. Nothing feels unmanageable.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay. Once the baby settles for the night I can usually drift off without trouble.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable—just tired sometimes, but that’s different.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all—maybe a couple happy tears when the baby first smiled at me, but not from feeling unhappy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel pretty steady.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Source: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) analogue interview (10 items)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Transient, situational worries about infant well-being (Q4)  
- Mild fluster when routine disrupted (Q6)

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, crying spells, sleep-onset problems unrelated to infant care, panic, self-harm ideation (Q1-3, 5-10)

Pattern  
Overall affect remains positive; retains capacity for pleasure, humour, and adaptive coping. No vegetative signs of depression. Anxiety is limited to brief, reality-based infant safety checks without escalation or functional impairment.

Screening significance  
Current responses place patient well below conventional EPDS clinical cut-off range for major postpartum mood disorder. No safety concerns identified. Continue routine paediatric and maternal follow-up; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
